blocks.vo_line: Something is about to happen to the Moon. And most people are going to sleep through it. August 28th. It goes dark, not all of it, and not for long.
This is the Corn Moon, the final one before autumn. Normally it just rises. This year, something gets in front of it.
The answer is Earth. For a few hours, our planet slides directly between the Sun and the Moon.

And here's the part people never think about. The shadow it casts is enormous, roughly one point four million kilometres long. The Moon orbits barely a quarter of the way out. So a dark bite grows across the surface, slowly at first, then all at once. No telescope. Nothing to set up. Just look up.

And there's something else. Two weeks earlier, the Sun went dark behind the Moon. This time, Earth returns the favor. Two eclipses, one fortnight. That's not coincidence. It's orbital mechanics lining up.
It peaks just after moonrise, visible across the Americas, Europe and Africa. Then the shadow slides off, and the Moon comes back like nothing happened.
So here's my question. When it happens, are you actually outside? Or are you scrolling, and seeing the photos tomorrow, wishing you'd looked?
Tell me below. I read every single one.
